\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Over $z\le1.8$, the distance-sector endpoint differs from both Planck references in nearly the same redshift-dependent way. Across the constrained bins, the RMS difference between C1 and C2 is approximately 1\% to 8\% of the corresponding difference between R and either Planck reference. The R–C1 and R–C2 difference fields share one dominant direction (cosine~\GeometryCosineSimilarity{}, principal angle \GeometryPrincipalAngle$^{\circ}$), with cross-reference transfer degradation fraction \GeometryTransferDegradation{} or less, reaching its largest amplitude near $z\sim\GeometryPeakZ{}$.

A five-coordinate order-3 reconstruction summarizes this difference with local projected Jacobian rank~5 of~5 fitted coordinates ($\chi^{2}=\BridgeChiTwo{}$). The matched constrained-domain bootstrap gives $P(\mathrm{select}\ge3)=0.216$, and the separate continuation to the Ly$\alpha$ anchor at $z=2.33$ fails.

The resulting empirical target is the redshift-dependent difference between the distance-sector history and the Planck-calibrated histories over $z\le1.8$. Its compact form now provides a concrete expansion-history pattern against which candidate physical explanations and independent observables such as growth, lensing, chronometers, time-delay distances, and standard sirens can be tested.
